Welcome to the dungeons interface!

This codex contains information about how dungeons work and how to edit and use them;  the available topics are listed on the left.

Do feel free to close this window and go just experiment with the available editing tools. You can explore this Codex whenever you want, from the "Dungeon Design" menu near the bottom right of the screen.

Often, players will want to attempt to complete a dungeon in order to defeat a dungeon boss.

Dungeon bosses are giant monsters which can engage in epic, multi-phase fights.  You can edit your bosses from the 'Bosses' option under the 'Dungeon Design' menu.

Bosses are very much like normal monsters, except that you can specify multiple phases for their fights, giving them custom health amounts and visual effects for each phase, and even script specific attack patterns for them to use in each phase.

If you leave a boss monster's attack patterns empty, they'll use default monster AI to select their own attacks.

You can specify the loot a boss will drop by selecting the placed boss in the dungeon layout.  These custom loot rewards can include gold, saleable loot, and even keys.
Dungeon must be offline to access
Dungeon must be online to access

Your players will need a way to get in and out of your dungeon layout.

Placing these is exactly like placing buildings on the world map;  just be sure you keep the entrance accessible within the dungeon layout!

When they're online, Dungeons run multiple instances so that different groups of players can be playing in them simultaneously.

In addition to a one-time setup cost, you'll need to pay a daily upkeep fee for each instance you have in each dungeon, whether it is being used or not.  It can be worth checking back to work out whether you need to change the number of instances your dungeons are running, as your number of subscribers change over time.

You can change how many instances you want to run for each dungeon using the 'Configure Instances' button, while the dungeon is online.

Note that it takes instances some time to reset themselves after each party has finished, but once that completes, the next party in the queue (if any) will be notified that the dungeon is ready, and they'll begin the journey to the dungeon.

Doors can be used to control how players explore a dungeon, as players will have to first collect a key for each door they wish to open.

There are two types of key and two matching types of door;  "normal" and "boss".

Any one normal key can open any one normal door, and any one boss key can open any one boss door.

You may place keys individually, loose on the floor inside your dungeon, or they may be set as a loot drop from a container, or as a custom loot drop from a boss.

Do be aware that your subscribers will be reading reviews and guides about your dungeon online, and will try to optimise their path through your dungeon; locked doors which don't have valuables behind them are unlikely to fool them and get keys spent on them!

Dungeons are an off-world-map space where parties of players can test their skills against specially-designed challenges, including terrifying boss monsters!

Dungeons can only be entered by parties of multiple players, so you must first enable the 'Parties' feature, if you haven't already done so.  The 'Parties' feature may be enabled in the 'Features' interface from the main Design menu.

When they are online, dungeons can demand a lot of bandwidth to run, so be sure that you give them a solid connection to your network infrastructure!

Dungeon floors can be painted;  you can select from several different materials and patterns and paint them directly onto the floor, to dress up your dungeon's appearance.

Most dungeon floor paints can be customised in many ways!

We provide a 'paint' and an 'erase' tool, along with an 'eyedropper' tool which will pick up the settings that were used to paint the floor in one location so that you may use precisely matching settings again somewhere else.

A dungeon can only be put into an 'Online' mode if it has a legal layout, which means it has:

1. At least three dungeon tiles.

2. An accessible dungeon exit.

3. At least one 'goal' (a piece of loot to be collected, or a boss to be defeated).

Note that normal and elite monsters do not qualify as 'goals'.

Additionally, note that an active dungeon will not be used by players unless they are able to form a party first, so the 'Parties' feature must be enabled before players will enter the dungeon.

Like most things in your MMO, a dungeon can be in one of three statuses:  Offline, Maintenance, or Online.

To edit a dungeon's layout, the dungeon must be in 'Offline' mode with all its instances shut down.

Your developers will automatically put the dungeon into 'Maintenance' mode when they're fixing bugs, which will shut down all dungeon instances, kicking out any players who were inside.  The developers will automatically return it to 'Online' mode when they've finished fixing bugs.

When in 'online' mode, the dungeon will create multiple playable instances of the dungeon, which parties of players will enter.

Please see 'Instances' for more details!

Note that in order to bring a dungeon online, the dungeon must contain at least three placed dungeon tiles, an exit, and at least one 'goal' for subscribers to achieve;  this might be a treasure to collect or a boss to kill.

Dungeons are constructed from tiles.  These tiles come in several different themes, and can be recolored if desired.

Additionally, when dungeon tiles are edited, we automatically populate the dungeon layout with scenery items to decorate it.  You can change how many of these scenery items you want us to place by adjusting the 'Autoprop Percentage' slider in the tool options, near the bottom right of the screen.

This is your main action bar.  Your various tools for interacting with the world will appear here.

You're all ready to go!

Feel free to keep working for as long as you like, but you're now ready to open your game and let subscribers begin to join.  To do that, click the 'Release' tab in the top right, and then the 'Announce Release' button.  GLHF!

Now we've selected 'Starting Points' as our technology to develop, we need to assign a developer to the project.

You can do that from the 'Staff' tab of the 'Development' window.  (If you've closed it, you can open it again from the 'Reports' menu at the bottom right of the screen).

On the 'Development' window, click on the small 'person' icon near the Starting Point development project to assign a developer to work on that project.  Some technologies can have more developers working on them, which will make them develop more quickly, but with more bugs.

Now we have the most critical buildings placed, but let's place some more useful items for players.  First, let's build a blacksmith near the inn.  Once players have some money, they will want to buy better weapons!

As before, place the blacksmith.  The network cabling controls are still enabled too, if you need to wire more bandwidth over to where you put the blacksmith.

Now that we have an uplink, we need to distribute the bandwidth it supplies!

Place a network cable using the highlighted tool, starting from the uplink.  You don't need to connect exactly to the respawn point;  as long as it's in the highlighted region around the cable, it's close enough!  Once bandwidth is running through the cable, it might take a few seconds for the respawn point to power up;  we'll continue once it's powered!

Now we have a reasonable starting region set up, with just one exception;  we need a starting point where players will enter the world!  Our developers have finished creating the 'Starting Points' technology for us, so let's integrate it into the game by going into the Development interface and clicking the 'DEPLOY' button.

Now lets place your newly developed starting point somewhere near your settlement in your starting region.

Once it's placed, we'll be ready to release the game!

Before we can begin designing our world, we'll need to activate one of these regions to become a starting region for new players.

Look around to find a region you'd like to use for that, and then go to the 'Grid' view by clicking the highlighted tab on the action bar.

By default, we only have one developer working for us;  now that we have assigned them to work on starting points, we won't have anyone to help us set up the MMO world, so let's hire a second developer!

Click the "Hire" button in the Development window to continue.

Next, let's build an inn somewhere near the respawn point.  Players will want to set a 'home' wherever they go, so you'll need at least one inn in each region you use.  Place one now.

Remember to make sure it has bandwidth available!  You can place more network cables if you need them.

Did you notice the little red cursor arrow which travelled to the Inn after you built it?  That was one of your developers, turning it on.  Developers need to visit every building you construct to enable them, and they travel via the nearest respawn point.  If your respawn points are very far away, this can take some time!

Players only know about places they've seen or heard about, but they can always see landmarks in the region, no matter how far away they are.

Place a landmark somewhere near your inn, so players can always see their way back home.

This is the main status display.  It tells you the name of your MMORPG, and some core information about it.

Right now you don't have any subscribers, but we'll fix that soon!

Now we should create some monster zones!  Monster zones require quite a lot of bandwidth, particularly if they're big.  You may need to run some extra network cabling out through them, to keep them online.  Click 'OK' and we'll get started.
Feel free to keep editing monster zones until you feel like you have enough, then click 'OK' to continue!

Okay, I've enabled the monster zoning tools for you, under the 'NPCs' tab.  Create a few large monster zones; I recommend each be about as big as three or four map squares, but feel free to go larger if you want!

You'll need to pick what monster to use, and then paint out regions on the map.

Okay, now that we've started development on starting points, let's get down to work on the game world itself;  you'll be able to watch the progress of starting points in the top right corner of the screen.

Close the Development window and click "OK" to continue.

The region you bought has turned green, and now has a number '1' in it.  This means that any content we build here will automatically be appropriate for characters of level 1.

Click 'OK' to continue.

These are the system buttons;  they provide information and access to design options, and allow you to save your game.

By the way, this game autosaves periodically, and when you exit.  You can change that behaviour in the game settings, if you like.

Finally, let's place a few quest giver NPCs.  Quest givers are how you give your subscribers things to do, which helps keep them from feeling lost!

Place two quest givers a little in front of your Inn, so players are likely to notice them.

You can edit your quest givers' quests, if you click on them and check their 'Quests' tab.  Feel free to play with that if you like!  Subscribers only have to kill about four monsters to reach level 2.

Click 'OK' to continue.

At the right side of the screen you'll see a task list for setting up this new region.  The first thing any region needs is a respawn point.  If a subscriber's character dies in combat, they'll automatically respawn from the closest respawn point.

What's more, developers and game masters can move around the game via its respawn points.

Notice how the respawn point you placed is dark and is showing an energy bolt icon?  That's because it doesn't have a network connection yet!  Let's set one up.

First, switch to the 'Network' view.

Since developers and game masters travel through respawn points;  having them near trouble spots can help your developers get work done more quickly!

Build a respawn point now, somewhere near the middle of the region.  You'll find the tool for placing one under the 'Buildings' tab.

Almost done!

Let's think about roads for a minute.  When a subscriber wants to go somewhere, they'll usually just run straight there, and this can send them through dangerous areas.  If you place roads, players will usually follow them, instead of cutting through areas.

Try placing a few roads, using the road-building tool now highlighted.

You can also rotate the camera.

While holding the right mouse button, move the mouse to rotate the view.

Here on the right edge of the screen is where we plan our development goals and game releases.

Click the 'Set Next Development Goal' button, and choose to start work on "Starting Points".

Finally, let's build a market stall.  Most of a player's gold will come from selling the vendor trash they take off defeated monsters.

Place a market stall, and make sure it has bandwidth to continue.

If you'd like to adjust the terrain of the region, it's easiest to do it now, before we start building things.

Each region has four terrain types that can be mixed within its borders.  Click on the 'Terrain' tab to see them, and feel free to experiment with them now. Click 'OK' when you're ready to continue.

Now that a region has been activated, let's go back to the main view.

Click the 'Interact' tab to return to the normal game view.

We have no network connection right now, so let's install a network uplink.  Use the highlighted tool to place one somewhere in this region.

Network gear is laid out underneath the terrain.  If you're placing it under large trees, you might need to zoom in if you want a better view.

Let's start with some basics.

Use the WASD or arrow keys to move the camera.

Welcome to MMORPG Tycoon 2!

Press 'OK' below to begin.  We'll cover basic movement, and then set up a bare bones game.

Back on the main map, the 'Grid' view shows us the current status of the game's region servers.  Right now they're all disabled, so let's activate one as a starting region.

Select the highlighted 'Activate Region' tool, and click on a region to activate it.

Next, let's get a closer view.

You can zoom in and out by scrolling the mouse wheel.

Zoom down to ground level, to continue.
Great!  Zoom out to view the whole map again, and we'll start looking at more of the game's interface.

In the 'Design' tool, you can customise both the appearance and also the combat abilities of your classes!

If you like, you can add new abilities which can be unlocked as your players gain levels.

You'll want to do this each time your subscribers reach a new level.

Subscribers will eventually become unhappy if there's no new content or quests for them to do at their new, higher level!

Set up the level 2 region in the same way you set up the level 1 region;  a respawn point, an inn, some monster zones, some quests.

When you're ready, open a mountain pass between your regions so that players can travel from one region to the other!  (Flight paths will work too, if you've unlocked them!)

Now that you have a level 2 player, you're going to need a level 2 region for them to play in!

If you haven't already, now would be a great time to go to the 'Grid' tab and activate a second region, next to your level 1 region!  Be sure to use the "Set Region Level" tool to set that region as a level 2 region!

And you're all ready to go!  Keep building regions out ahead of your highest level players and try to keep them busy and happy!

Or if not 'happy', then at least still paying their subscription fees, because at the end of the day, that's the only *really* important thing.

Click "OK" to capitalism!

If you do provide higher-level abilities for your players, you'll need some class trainers to teach players to use those new abilities!

You'll need trainers matching each of the player classes that you want to be able to learn the new combat moves you've created!
